_comment: Freshness policy: at what age does a stored price stop being something a shopper can act on? Data rather than code, for the same reason as feasibility.json — this is a judgement about groceries, not a fact derivable from the catalogue, and it should be reviewable by someone who knows about supermarket pricing rather than someone who knows about Python.
_decision_2026_08_30: RAISED FROM 14 TO 45, deliberately and reversibly, by Philip (service owner). WHY: the deployed dev endpoint is seeded with fixtures captured 2026-07-31. When version 6 of the Lambda began enforcing freshness on 2026-08-30, every priced query started returning STALE_DATA at 30 days of age — correct behaviour against data that had simply aged out, but it left the deployed endpoint unable to demonstrate anything priced. 45 days clears the 30-day fixture snapshot with a fortnight of headroom, so the demo does not break again mid-sprint. WHAT IT COSTS: 45 days spans roughly six weekly special cycles rather than two, so a comparison drawn at the limit of this window can be wrong in exactly the way the 14-day figure existed to prevent. This is acceptable ONLY because the dev stage serves fixture prices to the project team, not real prices to real shoppers. REVERT WHEN: real ingested prices with genuine capture dates back the serving table (Pilot Task 13) — at that point return this to 14, or to whatever the measured refresh cadence justifies, and do not carry 45 into any stage a shopper can reach. NOT A REVIEW: this is a demo-availability decision, not a judgement about grocery pricing, and it does not discharge the _review note below.
_revert_condition_re_read_2026_09_04: HELD AT 45, and the revert condition above needs restating rather than honouring. Its words -- 'revert when real ingested prices with genuine capture dates back the serving table' -- are now literally satisfied: the table holds 2,759 real Lineage B rows captured 2026-08-28, and the fixtures are out. But the condition was written expecting REFRESHED data to follow, and none can. LineageBSource.CAPTURED_AT is the constant '2026-08-28' and datasets/DATA_SCHEMA.md calls the collection a one-off snapshot, so no source available to this project can stamp a newer date; the weekly refresh rewrites the same rows with the same date (config/data-sources.json _what_the_weekly_refresh_is_actually_for). Reverting to 14 would therefore return STALE_DATA for every priced query from 2026-09-11 with no remedy short of a new snapshot -- not a stricter policy, just an outage on a date nobody chose. At 45 the same cliff arrives 2026-10-12. THE REAL REVERT CONDITION IS A SOURCE THAT CAN STAMP A NEW CAPTURE DATE: a fresh collection from the data team, or Task 11.4 live acquisition. Until one exists this number is buying time, and the honest reading of a held threshold is that the gap is in the DATA, not in the policy.
_why_not_restamp_the_fixtures: The rejected alternative was to rewrite the fixtures' valid_date to today so the data looked fresh. That fabricates provenance: those prices were invented on 2026-07-31, and stamping them with a later date asserts a capture that never happened. AGENTS.md lists 'publish a price without its capture date' under Do not, and the point of that rule is the date being TRUE rather than merely present. Raising a documented threshold is visible and reversible; rewriting a capture date is neither, and it would also make the staleness path impossible to test against real conditions.
_why_this_exists: The product's claim is not 'here is a price' but 'here is the CHEAPEST price'. A price can be merely out of date; a COMPARISON drawn from out-of-date prices can be actively wrong, because the winner changes when a special rotates. ACQUISITION-RISK.md finds the binding legal constraint is the Fair Trading Act, and that it attaches to the comparison we publish rather than to the fetch. So staleness is not a display problem, it is a claim we stop being entitled to make.
_what_happens: Records older than this are excluded before any comparison is built. If some are fresh, the comparison is made from those alone. If EVERY record for a request is stale, the turn returns STALE_DATA naming the newest capture date it found, rather than presenting an old comparison as current.
_calibration: ORIGINALLY 14 days, raised to 45 on 2026-08-30 — see _decision_2026_08_30. The original reasoning, which still governs what the number SHOULD be once real ingested data lands: 14 days. Supermarket specials in New Zealand rotate weekly, so a fortnight spans roughly two cycles: long enough that a normal refresh gap or a weekend outage does not refuse every shopper, short enough that a price which has since changed twice is not presented as today's. It is a starting position, not a measured one.
_what_it_is_not: Not a statement about how often ingestion SHOULD run — that is Req 8.4 and Pilot Task 13. This is the point past which the data we happen to hold stops being usable, which is a different question and deliberately a more forgiving number than the refresh interval.
_on_the_reference_date: Age is measured against an injectable reference date, not against the wall clock directly. Production passes today; tests pin a date at which the committed fixtures are fresh. Without that, fixtures captured on a fixed day drift into staleness as calendar time passes and every demo turns red on a date nobody chose — a test suite whose result depends on when you run it is not a test suite.
_review: This number has NOT been reviewed by anyone with domain expertise in grocery retail. Like min_grams_per_person_day it was set by reasoning rather than by evidence, and it decides which requests get refused outright, so it should not stay unreviewed indefinitely. Revisit it when real ingestion cadence is known: if refresh runs daily, 14 days is far more generous than it needs to be.
